common_name: Austin City Limits Lindheimer's Maiden Fern
scientific_name: Thelypteris ovata var. lindheimeri 'Austin City Limits'

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Texas native tolerates considerably more sun than typical woodland ferns once established.

directions: This selection was found growing in a sunny roadside cut in Comal County, Texas, just south of Austin, and stands out among ferns for tolerating considerably more direct sun than most of its relatives. Thick, upright, light-green fronds rise from spreading rhizomes to form a dense, deer-resistant patch that can reach several feet wide within a few years. Closely related to the widespread Thelypteris kunthii, it combines unusual sun tolerance with the toughness typical of Texas Hill Country ferns. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate or to control spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade; spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a broad groundcover colony over several years.

directions: This cultivar was raised from spores collected on Cheju (Jeju) Island off the coast of Korea and introduced by Plant Delights Nursery and Juniper Level Botanic Garden. Finely cut, light-green fronds rise upright from steadily creeping rhizomes, functioning as an elegant, deer-resistant groundcover that spreads into broad colonies over several years. It effectively serves as an Asian counterpart to the native New York fern, sharing a similarly delicate, finely divided texture. Give it part sun to light shade and evenly moist, humus-rich soil for the best coverage.

common_name: Weekend at Boerne Lindheimer's Maiden Fern
scientific_name: Thelypteris normalis var. lindheimeri 'Weekend at Boerne'

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; tolerates drier conditions than most ferns once established.

directions: This selection was discovered along Wasp Creek near Boerne, Texas, and grows roughly twice as tall as the typical form of this Lindheimer's maiden fern. Upright, gracefully arching, light-green fronds rise to about three feet, with the clump spreading slowly outward by stolons rather than aggressively colonizing rhizomes. It tolerates considerable sun exposure and even dry, sandy soil, making it unusually tough for a fern. Plant Delights and Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduced the selection in the mid-2000s.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; spreads over time to form a large, weed-suppressing patch.

directions: This selection of the Texas native Lindheimer's maiden fern was chosen for its vigor and was introduced by Plant Delights Nursery and Juniper Level Botanic Garden. Upright, deer-resistant, light-green fronds reach about three feet and spread outward by rhizomes to form a dense, winter-deciduous patch that can eventually cover ten feet or more. Although it is naturally found near water in the wild, it adapts readily to average garden moisture and tolerates both full sun and light shade. Use it as a bold, sun-tolerant groundcover mass where few other ferns would thrive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to shade; forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover patch over several years.

directions: This selection derives from a plant collecting expedition to Guizhou, China, and was introduced by Plant Delights Nursery and Juniper Level Botanic Garden. Upright, light-green fronds rise from densely spreading rhizomes to form a weed-proof groundcover patch, and the plant is unusual among ferns in tolerating full sun as well as light shade. Over time it forms broad, tightly knit colonies several feet across, making it useful as a large-scale groundcover for difficult sunny to shaded sites. Give it room to spread in average to moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade; vigorous enough to need sturdy companions rather than small, delicate groundcovers.

directions: Native to southeast China, this deciduous woodland fern was essentially unknown in cultivation before its introduction by Plant Delights Nursery and Juniper Level Botanic Garden. Mostly upright fronds rise from spreading rhizomes to form an attractive patch that goes dormant each winter and returns reliably in spring. It is vigorous enough to overrun small, delicate neighbors such as wild ginger or epimedium, so it is best paired with shrubs or larger woodland perennials that can hold their own. Site it in part sun to light shade with consistent moisture for the fullest effect.

planting.note: Plant divisions or crowns in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in part sun to shade; spreads quickly by rhizomes to naturalize large areas and grows shorter in regions with hot nights.

directions: This is the North American native botanical variety of ostrich fern, spreading quickly by rhizomes to send up new fronds every few feet and readily naturalizing large areas of moist ground. Like the familiar European form, it carries a central cluster of fertile, cinnamon-colored fronds amid the sterile vase of foliage, and it tolerates both consistently wet and surprisingly dry soils once established. In regions with hot days and warm nights it grows noticeably shorter than in cooler climates, so expect a more compact plant in southern gardens. It makes an excellent, fast-spreading native choice for naturalizing difficult damp shade.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part sun to shade; hardiness north of zone 7b is not yet well documented, so site conservatively.

directions: This naturally occurring Deparia hybrid was first described from Japan in 1977 and is also found in Korea, remaining uncommon in Western gardens. Narrow, upright, dark glossy-green fronds give it a distinctive fine texture quite different from the broader-leaved ferns typical of a woodland planting. It grows easily in average, slightly acidic soil in part sun to shade, though because it has been cultivated for such a short time, its true cold-hardiness limit is not yet well established. Site it conservatively within its known range until more garden experience accumulates.
